confidence_note: Principle 1 read directly in the publisher's excerpt. Year: first edition is 2005 (DB says 2004). The old text's networking pair, 'mirror' quote and Pygmalion link are not in the book and are dropped; the book's own two-people case is the Northridge commuters. Canfield co-wrote the book with Janet Switzer.
facts: Canfield learned E + R = O (Event + Response = Outcome) from Dr. Robert Resnick, a Los Angeles psychotherapist: every outcome follows from how you responded to earlier events.
Faced with an outcome you don't like, Canfield says you have two choices: blame the event, or change your response until the outcome changes.
Canfield lived through the 1994 Northridge earthquake in Los Angeles. Two days later he watched CNN interview commuters on a damaged freeway; a normal 1-hour drive had become 2 or 3 hours.
The first driver answered angrily: 'I hate California. First there were fires, then floods, and now an earthquake!' He said he would be late whatever time he left.
The driver in the car behind was all smiles. He had left home at 5 a.m. and had music cassettes, Spanish-language tapes, a cell phone, coffee in a thermos, his lunch and a book. 'It's no problem.'
Canfield: if the earthquake or the traffic were the deciding variable, everyone would have been angry. Leaving prepared or unprepared made the difference.
A friend's Lexus dealership in Southern California: when the Gulf War broke out, people stopped coming in. Newspaper and radio ads stopped working and sales fell steadily.

Of several new tries, the one that worked: driving a fleet of new cars to country clubs, marinas, polo grounds and parties in Beverly Hills and Westlake Village and inviting people to take a test drive. A high percentage bought or leased; they ended up selling more cars per week than before the war.
Canfield says you control only three things: the thoughts you think, the images you visualize and the actions you take.
scene_details: two cars in the same jam on a quake-damaged freeway, a CNN reporter knocking on each window
coffee in a thermos, Spanish-language tapes and a packed lunch on the passenger side
a fleet of new Lexus cars driven out to marinas and polo grounds
tension: Two drivers sat in the same traffic on the same morning; one was furious and one was fine, and the earthquake can't explain the difference.
opening_idea: Start at the car window: a CNN reporter, a freeway jam two days after the quake, and a driver listing fires, floods and the earthquake.

lessons.idea: When an outcome is bad, look for the part of your response you can still change before blaming the event.
lessons.anchor: The thermos driver and the dealership changed their response to an event they could not change.

lessons.idea: Prepared responses beat good luck in shared bad conditions.

reflect_final: Name a result you keep blaming on circumstances and one response of yours you could change before it happens next time.

use_cases.situation: The team blames the market for falling sales
use_cases.move: Mention the Lexus dealer who took cars to the marinas when nobody came in, then ask for one new response to test this month.

use_cases.situation: A friend is furious about a commute that keeps getting worse
use_cases.move: Ask what would go in the car if the delay were certain: coffee, a podcast, an earlier start.

use_cases.situation: You catch yourself complaining about the same thing for the third time
use_cases.move: Write the event, your usual response and one different response you will try next time.

pocket_idea: On the same jammed freeway, the driver with a thermos had a different day: change the response, not the traffic.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Two drivers in the same earthquake jam: one cursing California, one with coffee, lunch and Spanish tapes.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: CNN interviews two drivers after Northridge; then the Lexus dealer who drove cars to the rich instead of waiting; Canfield's E + R = O.
conversation_variants.question_idea: When did you change how you responded to something you couldn't change?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: Blame the event or change the response
